faq.answer: No. Employment duties, academic rank, licensure, community need, and unequal access may determine who teaches or holds credentials. Compare participation where formal status is removed.
faq.question: Do credentials or teaching establish social Type Five?

faq.answer: Use the same topic and person, then match invitation, audience familiarity, and decision authority. Differences that track hierarchy or access support an environmental explanation.
faq.question: How should knowledge roles be compared across groups?

faq.answer: Comfortable role-free participation, sharing incomplete ideas, accepting correction, and finding belonging outside expertise should all reduce confidence in this subtype account.
faq.question: What counterexample weakens the knowledge-role hypothesis?

sections.body_md: Within a Type Five hypothesis, the social subtype may emphasize contributing through a recognized field of knowledge or locating one's role through shared standards. This does not make expertise a personality essence.
sections.title: Frame expertise as a secondary relational observation

sections.body_md: Observe the same person sharing one topic with peers who have equal access and with a group structured by credentials or status. Compare participation after authority, invitation, and audience familiarity are matched.
sections.title: Compare the same knowledge across equal and unequal groups

sections.body_md: The social label organizes observations about roles and knowledge exchange rather than evidence about bodily mechanisms, neural organization, or an inborn social system.
sections.title: Keep group language non-mechanistic

sections.body_md: A person may enjoy gatherings, ask beginner questions, or contribute outside formal expertise while still using knowledge as one route into a group. Sociability level alone is not the construct.
sections.title: Allow ordinary sociability and broad participation

sections.body_md: Academic and professional hierarchies decide who may speak, whose knowledge counts, and which vocabulary signals membership. Education cost, language, disability access, discrimination, and seniority can shape participation.
sections.title: Examine credentialing and access before subtype

sections.body_md: Confidence should fall when the person participates comfortably without expertise, shares unfinished knowledge among peers, accepts correction without role threat, and builds belonging through activities unrelated to credentials.
sections.title: Challenge the hypothesis with role-free contribution

sections.body_md: Instrument-specific evidence cannot establish universal subtype ontology or cross-cultural equivalence. Record who grants authority and who bears exclusion before using this reversible hypothesis.
sections.title: Limit inference to the observed group context

sections.body_md:
Duration: 5

Context: Across five days, observe one peer group, one credentialed setting, and one informal community activity.

Observable signal: Record invitation, formal role, topic familiarity, vocabulary, who may correct whom, access barriers, and contribution made.

Page-specific signal: Compare the same knowledge exchange after authority and audience familiarity are held as constant as possible.

Alternative explanation: Check credentialing, academic hierarchy, professional duty, language, seniority, discrimination, and unequal access.

Reflection prompt: Find one role-free contribution that created belonging and use it to challenge the subtype hypothesis.

seo.description: Type Five social is a traditional subtype hypothesis about attention to a knowledge role, valued expertise, and how understanding is exchanged within a group. Teaching, credentials, specialized language, or selective participation does not establish subtype because academic hierarchy, professional duties, credentialing, unequal access, status rules, and community norms may produce the same pattern.
seo.title: Type Five social: a knowledge-role and group expertise hypothesis
